snapshots.name: John Field
snapshots.subtitle: An Irish laborer living near Baker Farm
snapshots.body: Thoreau visits him and his family sheltering from a rainstorm and tries, without much success, to persuade him that a simpler, less laborious way of living is available to him. Field's determination to work himself into a better situation the hard way stands in deliberate contrast to Thoreau's own experiment.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed baseline identity at first mention; no concealed identity or later plot development.

snapshots.name: the woodchopper
snapshots.subtitle: A Canadian woodchopper and post-maker, deliberately left unnamed
snapshots.body: A frequent visitor to the cabin, strong and unpretentious, who reads Homer with Thoreau's help despite having little formal education himself. Thoreau says he has too fitting and poetic a name to print it.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed baseline identity at first mention; no concealed identity or later plot development.

snapshots.name: Cato Ingraham
snapshots.subtitle: A formerly enslaved man who once lived near the pond
snapshots.body: Once held as a slave by a local landowner and given a plot of ground he was allowed to consider his own, his old cellar hole is one of the traces of former inhabitants Thoreau finds in the woods. Little else about his life survives in the neighborhood's memory.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed baseline identity at first mention; no concealed identity or later plot development.

snapshots.name: Zilpha
snapshots.subtitle: A formerly enslaved woman who once lived and spun near the pond
snapshots.body: She kept a small house in the woods and was known locally for her loud singing while she worked. Her home was later destroyed by soldiers during the war of 1812, an incident Thoreau records among the area's old stories.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed baseline identity at first mention; no concealed identity or later plot development.

snapshots.name: Brister
snapshots.subtitle: A formerly enslaved man who gave his name to a nearby hill
snapshots.body: Once enslaved by a local family before gaining his freedom, he and his wife Fenda lived in the woods where Brister's Spring and Brister's Hill still carry his name. Thoreau finds only scattered traces of their orchard and home left standing.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed baseline identity at first mention; no concealed identity or later plot development.

snapshots.name: Fenda
snapshots.subtitle: Brister Freeman's wife, known for telling fortunes
snapshots.body: Remembered locally as a good-natured fortune-teller, she lived with Brister in the woods near the hill that bears his name. Thoreau records what little survives of her reputation among the neighborhood's old stories.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed baseline identity at first mention; no concealed identity or later plot development.

snapshots.name: Wyman
snapshots.subtitle: A potter who once lived by the pond
snapshots.body: He supplied the neighborhood with earthenware from a home near the pond, a trade later continued for a time by his son. Little remains of the site by the time Thoreau settles there himself.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed baseline identity at first mention; no concealed identity or later plot development.

snapshots.name: Hugh Quoil
snapshots.subtitle: A reputed veteran who once lived in a hut in the woods
snapshots.body: Said locally to have served at Waterloo, he lived out his last years in a small hut near where Thoreau later builds his own cabin. He died before Thoreau moved to the pond, leaving only his abandoned dwelling as a trace.
snapshots.editorialBasis: Reviewed baseline identity at first mention; no concealed identity or later plot development.
